segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, It's This American Life. I'm Ike Sriskandarajah in for Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Pablo, does this feel like an Icarus story to you?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Maybe, potentially.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: What part?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Well, Icarus dies. Not that part.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: This is Pablo Manriquez, and he recently survived his own personal Greek tragedy. He's a reporter in Washington, DC. I've known him for years. And this all began when a ripped-open package showed up on his front stoop.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: It's late winter, 2022. I find a box outside of my apartment. Inside is a canvas, the four primary colors, a paintbrush, and a palette. It just seemed like a sign.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Yeah. And that's like-- what's the sign?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: It was just, I thought to myself, somebody painted every painting in the Capitol and the White House and the Department of Justice. All these agency buildings, they have oil paintings. And yet, in the 15 years that I've been in Washington, I've never met an oil painter.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He had this light bulb moment. That could be him.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: It wasn't the first time he decided to become a new Pablo. When we first met, he was doing PR work. But he decided he wanted to be a reporter no matter what. So at 37, he moved into a flophouse and began freelancing for small publications. And now he spends his days chasing down politicians in the halls of Congress. He made it happen. So with these art supplies, he began to imagine this other life for himself. And he made a Pablo kind of plan.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: So I was like, if I become an oil painter, I would basically be the only oil painter I know and, in some sense, have a monopoly on oil painting in Washington. You know what I mean? If you want an oil painting, especially a portrait, you have to come to me.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: What Pablo lacks in skill and experience he compensates for with heat-seeking opportunism and blinding self-confidence. It can rub people the wrong way, but I appreciate the hustle.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Pablo, it's so funny to me that you're trying to pick one career in-- I can say it --a dying industry by supplementing your income with another dying industry.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Reporting, an artist, it's like the two poorest. It didn't make any sense to a lot of people.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But it made sense to Pablo. Pablo looked down at the new tools in his hands and then tilted his head skyward. Even as Icarus did before him, he saw a way to soar where no mortal had dared to soar. Our show today, myths in real life. What happened next to Pablo, and other daring actions by mortals challenging their small lives. And a cameo by a real life god because the gods get mad if you don't include them, and I'm too busy to get smote. Not today, Hades. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: It's This American Life, Act 1, Icarus. So Pablo Manriquez, in Washington, DC, had received these art supplies, perhaps discarded by an Amazon package thief, or perhaps a gift from the gods. And he figured, there's all these big egos in town who would love to be memorialized in oil portraits. Well, I could do that for them. Even though Pablo himself had never painted a portrait in his life, or painted anything for that matter.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: I had a clear vision in mind of what I needed to do. I needed to learn how to paint a face.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Politicians have them. We can't sell a portrait without one. Pablo finds a YouTube channel called Paint Coach. It has a 10-minute crash course. He follows along. He starts moving paint around on the canvas, and he's hooked. In his head, he's already competing with the legends who are hanging on walls around town. He just needs a first subject to paint. It's got to be someone widely recognizable, someone distinct and iconic. So he picks Mitch McConnell.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: He's always had super, super loyal staffers. I mean, I imagine he's-- according to his book, The Long Game, he's run out all his enemies and installed all of his friends. So I was hoping to find Mitch McConnell fans to buy Mitch McConnell paintings. Another thing I did, I looked up on Etsy, I looked up on the typical places where you would go to buy an oil painting, and I couldn't find any oil paintings of Mitch McConnell. If I painted five paintings of Mitch McConnell in a week, I had the only five paintings of Mitch McConnell in existence for sale. Right?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: After a few tries, he gets one that looks enough like Mitch McConnell. So he posts a few pictures of his progress, and someone notices. The next day--

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: I was walking through the Senate, and one of his aides kind of came out of the woodwork and was just like, hey, man, these paintings of our boss that you're posting on Instagram are really cool, but could you maybe paint him smiling? I was just like, boom. Hell yeah, I can paint him smiling. I can paint him smiling all day long.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Have you ever had a picture in your office of your boss smiling at you? If you have, you might be living in a country where the name "leader" is preceded by "great" or "supreme." I'd like to take this moment to say, I am grateful to work here at This American Life, where the company reimburses half the cost of the smiling portrait of Ira that we are forced to hang in our offices.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Pablo delivers his first smiling Senator to Mitch McConnell's staffer. And then he gets a request for another, and another. He's 18 Mitch McConnells deep before he stops to catch his breath.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Were those Mitch McConnells-- in your opinion, were they good?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: I can't think of a single Mitch McConnell I ever did that was good.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But they were good enough. He sold the first small one for $25, the next one for $50. Eventually, he settled on $500 for 24-by-36-inch paintings. Pablo is becoming a prolific painter. He paints Nancy Pelosi, Ilhan Omar, other politicians. He takes a commission for a lobbyist's dog. Just by his own force of personality, he's making it happen.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: At the State of the Union, Pablo set up an easel in Statuary Hall. That's overlooking where all the members of Congress and the Supreme Court justices pass through. And Pablo, in his white painter's coat with headphones on, he captured the scene on canvas live.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: This is something that is a side project of yours?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: C-span interviewed him as he painted. And then late last year, in December, he got a phone call from a friend's number, someone who used to be a policy advisor in the executive branch.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: I picked up. And I was just like, hey, man, what do you need? I'm kind of busy. I hear on the other end of the line, hey, Pablo, you're a great artist. This is Joe Biden. I'm like, bull-[BLEEP], man. Very funny, right? He's like, no, no, no, I'm serious. Hey, Jill, put it on FaceTime. And bloop, bloop bloop. The FaceTime noise plays. And I'm looking at Dr. Jill Biden.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: And I'm like, oh my God. I'm so sorry, ma'am. I'm so sorry for cursing. I did not mean to say BS in front of you. Yeah, this is real. And she hands the phone back over to Joe Biden. And he was just like, you're a really good artist. This is a really great portrait of Jill and me.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: If you've been wondering what Joe Biden's been up to since leaving office, well, mystery solved.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: He knew the photo that it came from. It was from the 1970s, when they first met. So it was an oil painting of them when they were young. And I was on FaceTime with the president. There were probably 25 reporters in the press gallery filing their stories. And pretty soon, they were all gathered around me. And we were all talking to Joe Biden-- The Washington Post, the AP, the Bloomberg, HuffPost, were all talking-- and Fox News, Daily Caller, we're all looking into the camera and talking to Joe Biden. And he's just telling everybody how bomb my painting is. I was like, that was awesome. That was awesome.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: This is the part of the story when Icarus, with wings cobbled together with wax and feathers, experiences the miracle of flight. Hey, I can see my Minotaur from here. Well, for many mortals, this level of success is thrilling and enough. But not for Pablo. Pablo has a bigger goal. He wants one of his paintings officially hung in the Capitol, approved by a committee and hung by an entity known as the architect of the Capitol, the only people allowed to drive a nail in the wall. Pablo wants to be immortalized in these halls of power.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: I have no legacy. Like, you know what I mean? And while no one might remember any story I write ever, right, the painting will be there for centuries. Centuries, if it's on the wall.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Maybe you've been wondering this whole time, what do these paintings look like? So to be totally honest, Pablo has improved a lot. But he's doing work that looks like it's made by a talented art student, maybe a folk artist. The colors are pleasing. You can always tell who it is he's painting. But it's not, you know, John Trumbull's painting of the founders signing the Declaration of Independence, or any of the other museum grade paintings hanging in the Capitol rotunda.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Of course, that does not stop Pablo, and a couple of months ago, he saw a way to make his dream happen. In February, the House voted to rename the press gallery after Frederick Douglass, who, among many other things, was also the first Black reporter to cover the Capitol. There was going to be a renaming ceremony and press conference. Well, it just so happened that Pablo had made a portrait of Frederick Douglass. It had been leaning against the wall in the press gallery for the last two years. So Pablo quickly hatched a plan. He's going to grab his painting, sneak his painting into the room where the ceremony is going to take place, and slip it onto a table where everyone can see it.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: I scoped out the room. I was like, oh, there are artifacts about Frederick Douglass here. Like, there was this ledger of sales and stuff like that under glass. I was like, I'm going to go grab my painting and put it on the table. And I did. It's like a pop art portrait of Frederick Douglass with a yellow background, like a distinct yellow background.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: It's a pretty big canvas, nearly life-sized. And it sticks out compared to, say, the items on loan from the Library of Congress. But nobody says anything. Then the VIPs come in. There's the Speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, Representative Byron Donalds, the bill's sponsor. And there's even a living descendant of Frederick Douglass. Traditionally, at a press conference like this, the press are there to cover the event, not insert themselves into it. But Pablo is Pablo.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: And when Mike Johnson came in, I showed it to him. I showed it to Byron Donalds. He's like, oh, yeah, there. And that's when Frederick Douglass's grandson was like, that's great, that's great.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Probably not grandson.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: And then he kept walking. I was like, OK, so Frederick Douglass's grandson is cool with this. Byron Donalds is cool with this. Speaker Johnson is cool with this.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He gets a selfie with the lawmakers and his painting.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Everybody loves the painting. So let's get it hung on the wall officially.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: To do that, Pablo just needs the permission of something called the Standing Committee of Correspondents. These are a group of Pablo's own peers, other working journalists. So he writes them a letter, donating his painting to the committee and asking that they hang it in the newly-named Frederick Douglass Press Gallery. A couple weeks later, the Standing Committee of Correspondents meet. The first new business on the agenda that day is to take a vote regarding artwork.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: And they voted no. They said no. I was just like, oh. I still don't know exactly why.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Did you ask any of them?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Pablo was not discouraged by this decision. Of course he wasn't. He was like, well, if they don't like this Frederick Douglass, I'm going to make them a much bigger Frederick Douglass. And if they don't like that, I'll paint a smaller one. And I'll keep painting and donating Frederick Douglasses until the dam breaks and they all go up. I thought that sounded like a lot of work, at least more than asking them why they said no.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: So I reached out and got hold of the meeting minutes. The problem was not about the size or the quality or anything like that. The problem was that Pablo had crossed a line.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The thing that they voted on wasn't at all about your painting, but a broad rule that would apply to all future situations.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: What was the rule, don't bring a painting?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: No, it's not, don't bring a painting. Is that no credentialed reporter will be able to make artwork that hangs on the walls of the Capitol. Is this the first time you're hearing that?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Yeah. And that's written down?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Yeah. It was a 4-to-1 vote. And how does that make you feel?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Kind of sad.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: According to a statement from the Standing Committee, they were worried about what precedent it would set, what conflicts of interests hanging his painting could cause. And Pablo hadn't gotten permission from the event organizers to put his painting into their event.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Icarus, son of Daedalus, soaring over the Isle, was enthralled by his own new ability. He couldn't help wanting to go higher. Pablo, son of Luis, didn't want to only stay in the back of the press conference with the other scribes. Couldn't this event to honor Frederick Douglass also honor Pablo, too? Maybe if he'd asked permission, gone through channels, this all might have worked out differently. I floated that idea by Pablo.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Was there another way to do it? Yeah. But I still think this was the best way.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Even when you're thinking about it now, reflecting on it?

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Yeah, because humility could not possibly have created that scenario to begin with. At every point along the way, it was driven by ego.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: A lot of it was ego.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: Maybe like 91%, 92%. I definitely wake up every morning excited to be Pablo Manriquez.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Ego-- it's what makes you pick up a box of stolen art supplies and think, without any experience, I will be a transformational force in the US Capitol. But it's also ego that propels you to the front of a press conference, with your painting under your arm, and sends you crashing back to Earth. The Potomac is lousy with wax and feathers.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: A couple hours after we talk, Pablo sends me a note. He's back in the Capitol. He says, for the first time, he feels small in this place that once made him feel big. The next day, he sends me another note. He sounds like himself again. He figured it out. He's launching his campaign to run for Standing Committee.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: But luckily, I'm not eligible to run for the Standing Committee for at least another year, if not two. So I decided that, while I can't be on the ballot until probably 2028, I am going to start campaigning on Monday. So I registered the domain dailypressgallery.com, and I started writing an agenda. Part of my agenda is, of course, to repeal the prohibition that they put on journalist art in the Capitol.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: You never hear about Icarus the next day. Did you know he just made some small adjustments to his wings and headed right back for the sun?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: If you want to see Pablo's paintings or follow his campaign for Standing Committee, he's at Pablo.Manriquez on Instagram.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That brings us to act two, Cerberus.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: You know how in Greek mythology there's Hades, where everyone goes when they die? You gotta cross the River Styx to get there. And then there's this gate with this three-headed dog, Cerberus. He's guarding the entrance, and he's supposed to make sure only actually dead people enter. This story is about a real person in America who stood at those very gates, which is not the easiest job, it turns out. At least not right now. Nadia Reiman talked to him about it.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: When Jeremiah Schofield started working at the Social Security Administration, the SSA, the first thing his boss said to him was, if you're looking up your ex's records, your own records, or looking up someone famous, don't. We will know. Then they made him read Title V of the US Code Section 552a, The Privacy Act, the actual legal text of it. That's how much they wanted to drive the point home.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: The Social Security Administration is the caretaker of these truly massive databases of personal information. They use it to send Social Security checks, disability payments. And in order to do that accurately, given how there's over 300 million of us, they keep master files. Jeremiah says they have all sorts of information from all sorts of moments in your life-- where you were born, your Social Security number, your mom's maiden name, your citizenship status, all of it stored in giant files.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: Your master earnings files will show every job that you ever worked at. And it would show how much money you made at all of those different jobs.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Every job people have had?

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: Yep. And then you have the disability control file, which actually gets into disability-related information.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: That's for people who collect disability.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: Things like what your disability-- there's listings of codes for if you have cancer or if you have some other type of ailment. And so it would have all of that information in it. So it's very sensitive information. At Social Security, we've always treated those records as though they're things that they cannot be let out to anybody.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Like, they contain people's whole lives, basically.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: That's right. Very sensitive moments in their lives.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: The point of the many rules governing these lists and files is not just privacy, though. It's about making sure all this information is used only for its intended purpose, by the book. And Jeremiah, from what I can tell, is a by-the-book kind of guy.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: There's one database with arguably more power than the others and a name to match. It's called the Death Master File. It's a master list of all the dead. Well, all the deaths recorded since the dawn of Social Security.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: It has millions and millions of names. People get added to it when they die, their name and their date of death. If you get accidentally added to it when you are not dead, it can mess up your Social Security payments, sure, but also your bank accounts, all kinds of things. So Jeremiah and everyone treated this one with extreme care.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: And one day, Jeremiah says, he was summoned to a meeting. And the first thing he sees when he enters the meeting room, handwritten on all these whiteboards, are the names of all these databases, including the Death Master File.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: The whole meeting was kind of strange, actually. Jeremiah was a boss. At this point, he had been there 25 years, his first proper adult job. So he'd been to a lot of meetings, but none like this. It was not put on the official calendar, and the whole thing was very secretive. It was in a half-used office building. There was a guard in the hallway, almost like a bouncer. And in the room, three people with non-government laptops.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: This was February of last year. And these guys, they worked for DOGE, so-called Department of Government Efficiency, headed by Elon Musk. In the meeting, Jeremiah makes some proposals, some ways Social Security can be more efficient, better IT to update these lists quicker. But he's almost instantly interrupted by one of the DOGE guys, Antonio Gracias, a venture capitalist, now Team Elon.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And within two minutes, Mr. Gracias had shut down the conversation and said, we're here to talk about Social Security fraud. And we're looking for a big win. And I said, well, a big win? I mean, I have millions of dollars in potential savings by doing these new IT systems. And he said he was only willing to go to the president with a big win of-- he said $50 billion savings.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: What did you say?

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: Well, what I said was that I don't think you're going to find $50 billion in fraud.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Around this time, Elon Musk announced on X that they might have found some fraud. The fraud was related to the Death Master File. Musk was pointing to a problem with it, namely that there were people who were clearly dead who were not in it, people who seem to be 150 years old, according to other Social Security databases. He posted, quote, "Maybe Twilight is real and there are a lot of vampires collecting Social Security." He even brought it up in the Oval Office with President Trump, before the cameras.

segments.speaker: Elon Musk
segments.text: Now, do you know anyone who's 150? I don't. OK? They should be on the Guinness Book of World Records. They're missing out.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Jeremiah saw all this.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: So in layman's terms, I was pissed off that our leaders in the country were saying this. And it was infuriating.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Jeremiah was pissed off because, in layman's terms, [BLEEP]'s complicated. It's true that there were some people who appeared to be 150 not marked as dead, but the Social Security Administration knew that already. And they knew why. Sometimes the death of a person born in 1875 or whatever didn't get reported to the SSA. And without an official death date, that person didn't go on the Death Master File.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Regardless, there was a whole system in place to make sure Social Security payments did not go out to these people. Because when someone is over 100, the Social Security Administration actually contacts them to make sure they're still alive.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And so we have different groupings of technicians within the agency that literally make phone calls to these folks, and in some cases go to people's houses just to make sure-- hey, Jeremiah is over 100 years old. Let's make sure that he's still living and that he's receiving the benefits that he needs to.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: He says some of these 100-plus year olds are happy to have a visitor. Others are like, go away, of course I'm alive. And if there's any fraud, anyone taking in a paycheck for a dead relative, the SSA would catch it. Plus, the SSA had already tried to clean up the Death Master File, specifically chasing down death dates for these 150-plus year olds. But it took a lot of time and resources, and it didn't save the government any money, because it's not like the SSA had been sending checks to these dead people. So the opposite of efficiency.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: But DOGE still pressed on. They wanted Jeremiah's team to mark these apparent 150-year-olds as dead and mark them now. Just populate the sensitive list with random death dates, which was totally unheard of. And it made Jeremiah a little nervous It seemed like a bad precedent because, remember, if you make a mistake in the Death Master File, say, mark someone dead who isn't, it's not just their Social Security that gets shut off. Anything tied to their Social Security number is now bricked.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: The person finds out, often in pretty dramatic fashion, that they have been killed off by accident. Like, they go to the grocery store, they try to pay with their credit card, and it doesn't work. Then they try to pay with another credit card. Same thing. So they go home and call the bank. And they're like, what's going on?

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And they would have been directed to go to Social Security to fix the problem.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Could they have access to their money in their bank accounts or no?

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: The bank accounts would have been frozen.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Oh my God. So it's not even that they can't use credit cards. They can't take money that they have in the bank out of the bank at all.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: That's right. Everything just stops because everybody thinks that the person is deceased.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: It's a mess. And now here was DOGE, insisting Jeremiah's team marked these 150-plus year olds as dead. Jeremiah was like, OK, I know we don't have physical proof, but if the date of birth is right, logic says these people are for sure dead. So it didn't seem that risky.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: They did it methodically, carefully, to avoid making mistakes. But ultimately, they put in fake death dates for all those people. Jeremiah didn't like it, but he did it anyway.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: This fixation with the Death Master File, little did Jeremiah know it was just beginning. A few weeks after the 150-year-olds, Jeremiah says his higher-ups contacted him with a request from DHS, the Department of Homeland Security. And this request was unlike anything Jeremiah had seen in his more than 20 years at the agency.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: I got a request from the Deputy Commissioner for Operations, my boss, and said, we have a listing of a little over 6,000 people. You need to come up with a strategy on how we're going to kill off these 6,000 folks, a listing we had received from DHS.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Kill off? Like--

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: Yeah, DHS had sent us a list. And the expectation was is that we add a date of death for these individuals.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: To add these 6,000 or so names to the Death Master File. It was strange because, normally, deaths are reported by funeral homes or family members or some state authority. And also, there was no indication from DHS that these people were dead. They just said, add these people to this list. So Jeremiah and his colleagues were trying to figure out, what's going on, and why these 6,000 in particular?

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Like, oh, is a pattern here? Is it all people from one area of the country? There was nothing like that that you were able to see.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: I did not see it. But there were conversations that happened. And the conversations that happened around the agency indicated that it was mostly Hispanic last names.

segments.speaker: Pablo Manriquez
segments.text: DHS also sent a memo from then-Secretary of Homeland Security, Kristi Noem, about, quote, "suspected terrorists" who she said had Social Security numbers and access to our financial system. She asked the SSA to stop it in a way that was, quote, "consistent with law." Jeremiah was pretty sure none of this request to mark 6,000 people as dead was lawful. No proof of death, for one thing. So he says, he goes and asks someone at the Social Security office of General Counsel, the lawyers, who tell him, yes, it is illegal.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: The illegal part of it is is making them all dead. You can't just make anybody dead that's not dead. That's against the law.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: So Jeremiah and his team refuse. But then, within a couple of days, they start getting some strange reports from the field offices, workers calling in saying, what's going on? People are showing up here saying we marked them as dead. They're definitely not dead.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: I'm like, did somebody process these 6,000 deaths? And we started to ask around the agency at headquarters, and we found out that there was staff in the Office of Chief Information Officer that had posted the dates of death.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: He knew the Chief Information Officer staff did it because that was the only office that could process these deaths the way they were processed, all at once. Jeremiah says all 6,000-some people had been marked as having died on a single day, March 8, 2025. He couldn't believe they had done this.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: I mean, by the agency choosing to do this, we just took a list without any documentation, and we posted these 6,000 deaths. That could have happened to anybody. And within 48 hours, that anybody would have had their lives halted until they could fix it. And it's possible they could fix it in a few days. Or there's been cases where we've seen where it takes months or even a year to fix all of the little things that get screwed up because you got your name on the Death Master File.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: The process of getting resurrected-- that's what they call it when you're accidentally killed in the Death Master File and need to be brought back to life-- it's not simple. You have to go into your Social Security office in person and prove you're alive. And sometimes it takes multiple visits, as you keep encountering new corners of your life where some institution or other is still convinced you're dead.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Jeremiah doesn't tell the field offices that the 6,000 or so were secretly killed by the Chief Information Officer's office, or that DHS requested it. He's like, let's not dwell on the mess. Let's just fix it. And let's fix it the way we normally would, as any other mistake in the Death Master File. Which meant it was up to each one of these 6,000 or so people to come into their local field office and prove they're alive.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: We saw 30 resurrections happen pretty quickly. And then that number quickly grew within a few weeks to 300 resurrections.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: So that's what was happening on the ground. Meanwhile, from above--

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: We were getting pressure to say, we told you to kill off the 6,000. We want the 6,000 to remain dead.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: DHS was telling you that they wanted the 6,000 to remain dead.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: That's right. And it was coming down from pretty high up leadership.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: When these 6,000 fake deaths happened, The Washington Post found out and published a big story. So did The New York Times. So as the news breaks, Jeremiah is also dealing with the chaotic media fallout of this. And then something bigger happens. And this part of the story has not been out there before. Jeremiah is the first person to talk about it.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: So then fast forward a few weeks, and a new request comes in to kill off a new grouping of people. The new request from DHS is for 2.7 million names.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: DHS wants the SSA to kill off 2.7 million people, like an entire city, mark them all as dead in the Death Master File. Again, like last time, no sign or pretense that they're for real dead. DHS tells Jeremiah's team that these 2.7 million are here illegally, and also--

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: These folks were violent criminals and suspected terrorists.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: But, wait, they told you there were 2.7 million violent criminals and terrorists? That's a lot of violent criminals and suspected terrorists.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: It is. We were pretty suspect about this 2.7 million list. And so when it came in, we also thought it was a pretty big number. And we wondered whether or not the list was accurate.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Last time this happened, when Jeremiah said, wait a minute, these people are alive, that didn't stop the SSA from marking them as dead. So this time he tries something different. He decides to fact check the claims DHS made about the 2.7 million. They can't look at all 2.7 million people. Privacy concerns, and also, the number is so large. But they do get permission to look at a random sample from the list, 25 people. They check what they can.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And so we went through to check one, are they dead? Two, are they here legally or not legally? And what is their current status?

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: When Jeremiah's team ran the numbers, they found that all 25 from the sample were alive. And what's more--

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: When we went through the 25 records, we found 23 of them were records where people were either US citizens or lawful permanent resident or were here legally. And then there were two that more investigation needed to occur because it appeared as though that their alien status had expired.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: So, alive. And also, most of them clearly in the country legally. Here's what else he remembers from the sample.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: But I do remember that it did span a pretty big age community. So it was children all the way up to people in their 70s. There's a couple of cases that I remember that we just thought were super curious. There were some teenagers on the list. And we're like, OK, so teenagers are suspected terrorists and violent criminals? I mean, I guess that could happen, but the likelihood of it happening didn't make sense.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And then there was another person on the list that was a person that had been in the United States for over 50 years and was receiving widow benefits. And we're like, OK, so this person's a violent criminal and a suspected terrorist?

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: So Jeremiah is like, one, I can't mark people who are alive as dead. Two, they told us these were all people without status, and that seems to not be true. And three, the data I did see from the list makes me side-eye that they're even criminals. Too many red flags in a row. He decides to sound the alarm.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: I went to my boss. And my boss at the time was now Stephen Evangelista. He had taken over after my other boss left the agency. And I said, we need to have a meeting with DHS. And we need to talk through a couple of things because we think their list is inaccurate. And that's probably a light way of saying that.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: So he calls this meeting. They get DHS on a video call. And on the call, Jeremiah says they present their findings, that the people on the list are alive and seem to be here legally. DHS is like, OK, we'll get you a new list. But Jeremiah has another question. "Logistically," he asks, "if there are mistakes on this or any other list you give us, how would a person on the list by mistake fix it?"

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: And Jon Koval, a DOGE guy at DHS, says, "They would go in person to an SSA office, same as any other mistake. Oh, but when they get there, just flag them over for ICE." Jeremiah says he looked at his coworker, and they were visibly really uncomfortable. ICE is not a place where immigrants who have a mistake on any kind of government papers go to get them straightened out. It's where they go get deported. Jeremiah looks at his boss, Stephen Evangelista. To Jeremiah, DHS's intention is now crystal clear.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And so we were like, OK, thank you for the information. We wrapped up the call. Then we're still in the room. And I look across the table. I remember sitting across the table from Stephen. And I said, "The reason that they're doing this with this 2.7 million is because they're trying to deport all of these people. It's plain and obvious." And Stephen said, "You don't know that. You can't be sure of it. That's too much conjecture. You don't know this definitively."

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And I'm like, "Come on. We know this. This is why this is happening." He's like, "You just don't know it." So we got into a little back-and-forth in reference to that. And he's like, "OK, how about I just call Jon, and I'll ask him?"

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Jon Koval, the DOGE guy working with DHS.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: I'm like, "OK." He's like, "I'm going to call Jon. You guys be quiet." So "you guys" were me and his technical assistant. And, "I'll just have a quick conversation with Jon in reference to this 2.7 million and why." So he pulls out his cell phone, and he calls Jon. He puts Jon on speakerphone. And he says, Jon, can you tell me why we're going through all this effort with these 2.7 million people?

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And Jon said matter of fact terms back. He's like, "Well, there's two outcomes that we're hoping for here. One, we'll make the people's lives so miserable with-- their lives will just be hard to go through because we'll turn off their credit. We'll turn off their credit card. We'll turn off their bank. They'll just want to self-deport. Or two, they'll go into a Social Security office, and we'll have ICE pick them up there. Or you'll refer them over to us, and ICE will pick them up either at USCIS or at ICE, wherever you determine that they should go." Just matter-of-factly.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: And when he said that, I was shocked that he said it so matter-of-factly. I was pretty shocked that that happened. It's one thing to think you know and be like 98% sure, but you don't really know something. It's different when you know it 100% and you just heard it from a chief official over at DHS who also happens to be a DOGE associate. And he made it very plainly clear that this is what he was trying to do and the outcomes that they were seeking.

segments.speaker: Jeremiah Schofield
segments.text: Stephen was like, thank you for the information, quickly got off the call. My office, I had to go through a different door than Stephen did, out the conference room. He quickly got up. We didn't talk about it. We didn't have an after-the-meeting conversation about it. That was also a little bit shocking because I'm sure my face said, I told you so, in unequivocal terms. And so he got up. He went to his office. I got up, went to mine. And we never talked about it again.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: Jeremiah quit the SSA few months later, and now he's filing a whistleblower complaint. The 2.7 million person list was a crisis averted. The SSA didn't add those names to the Death Master File. As far as Jeremiah can tell, they're still alive. But of course, they always were.

segments.speaker: Nadia Reiman
segments.text: The government is filled with things like the Death Master File, built for one purpose, but if you're of a certain disposition, usable for something else. A list of the dead, a public service to track who is alive and who is dead, or a tool to kill off anyone you don't like. It's not legal. It flies in the face of rules and laws that have governed the list for decades. It violates the whole name of the list. But that doesn't mean you can't do it anyway.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Nadia Reiman is a producer on our show. By the way, we did reach out to all the people and agencies Jeremiah names in this story. Only the Department of Homeland Security got back to us. They gave us a statement saying, quote, "The government is finally doing what it should have all along, sharing information across the federal government to solve problems." Two congressional offices are currently looking into the allegations Jeremiah made in his whistleblower claim.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Coming up, one man will suffer through many ordeals to have a private encounter with a God living here on Earth, specifically in Barcelona. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ike Sriskandarajah. Today's show, Not Today, Hades. Our last act, Act 3, Zeus. He has taken many forms here on Earth. For the last 20 years, millions have been worshipping a man they say performs miracles. They call him many names-- Magician, Messiah, The Chosen One. And he looks, in some ways, kind of anonymous, like nobody special. He's short, 5' 7". He's soft spoken, shy even. The legends about this man are many. But very few of his devotees have ever actually met him, let alone talked with him.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Writer Daniel Alarcón is one of them, one of the very few mere mortals to have met Lionel Messi, arguably the greatest soccer player of all time. Daniel talked about it on the podcast he hosts with his longtime friend, who's also a writer, John Green. Daniel adapted it for our show.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: So John, once upon a time, there were many, many magazines that were published in the United States and around the world. As you know, I've written for many of them. And magazines, for our younger listeners, are very thin little books.

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: It's like Instagram, but text-based and printed.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Yes. And there was a specific niche among these that were called glossies. And glossies were the high-end fashion magazines. And the glossies got their name from the glossy paper that they were printed on. So Vanity Fair, GQ, Vogue, those are the glossies. And they were kind of lucrative.

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: Yeah, they paid great.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: They paid so much money. I had never written for a glossy magazine, I should say, until one of these editors who worked at one of these magazines called me up and asked me if I was interested in writing a profile of Lionel Messi. And of course, I was interested, huge soccer fan, blah blah blah. The problem is that I was about to be married, and the reporting trip would be the week after my wedding.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: So terrible timing. I was told I would get to spend three days with the world's greatest player. I'd get to see a training session. I'd get to go to a game. I'd have full access. And I spoke with Carolina. And she said, you've got to go, you got to do this, and we would do the honeymoon later. And I think you know this, but I think it's worth repeating, just what a genius Lionel Messi is, spoken of in the same breath as Pelé, as Maradona.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: And I felt like there are people who watch Lionel Messi play a game, and they're like, man, he's good. And there are people like me, who understand it or feel like we understand it on a completely different level. And I thought that there would be a way that I could express to him that my understanding of what he was accomplishing on the pitch was not like, woo hoo, goal. You know? It was a much more sophisticated understanding. And I was like, yeah, no doubt, me and Leo are going to be friends.

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: That's totally realistic.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: I was imagining us hanging out at his house, playing Xbox or FIFA or something, and then going to eat some Argentine barbecue somewhere, the grill in Barcelona somewhere, and then riding in his car. And then at the end of the night he'd be like, you know what, man? You're so cool. Cancel your flight back. We're hanging out.

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Normal stuff. So this is what I was imagining. And, yeah, so basically, 36 hours after my wedding, I'm on a plane to Barcelona. I arrived at New York. So I flew from San Francisco to New York. I checked my email. And that's when I got the first blow, which was that I would no longer have three days with Lionel Messi. I would have a single day.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Now, I still thought a single day is good. I was like, a day. That's still pretty good. I checked my email again when I got to Barcelona, and now it was no longer a day. It was an hour. So at this point, just to be clear, I had given up my honeymoon to spend an hour with a soccer player. It was just beginning to dawn on me that this was the wrong way to start my marriage, right?

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: So here's what happened. I got to Barcelona. I had planned four days in town. Now I've got two extra days to report. So I'm just going to report the [BLEEP] out of this story, which is what I do. So I talked to everybody. I found the guy who took Messi's first photo ID back when Messi was a teenager with long hair and he needed his ID card so he could enter the grounds of the stadium. I found the owners of the Argentine restaurant in the suburb where Messi has his gigantic home. And I got to sit in the booth where Messi sometimes goes to eat.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: So anyway, I finally do have my day where I'm going to go meet Lionel Messi. And I'm told to get to the Cuitat Esportiva around 10:00 AM. And of course, I did. Punctually there.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: And I get there, and I'm like, hey, so I'm a journalist for this fancy glossy magazine. This was all been scheduled. Publicists, editors have been negotiating my arrival. Can I walk around? No, no. No, you can't. I'm like, OK. And they take me to this kind of press room. And they tell me Messi will be there in a few minutes.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: It's super hot. This is like September. I was not given so much as a glass of water. And I waited, and I waited, and I waited. And then someone came in and told me that I'd be meeting Messi actually, not then, but before afternoon training. And I was like, OK. So can I watch the training? And they're like, no, absolutely not. You cannot watch the training. And I'm just like, what the hell? I'm like, what is this?

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: So I kind of like am peeking out the window. And I see Messi and the other players arrive. They have super fancy cars. And naturally, Messi did not come up to speak to me before training. And a little factotum was sent up to tell me that he would come after training. So at this point, training started at 3:00. I've been there, remember, since 10:00.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: I've resorted to going to the bathroom and just lapping water into my mouth out of the sink because I have not been given anything. That's nothing. I'm eating wadded up paper towels, just chewing on paper just to trick myself. I'm starving. And then I didn't know what had happened at training that day. I found out later. But I could tell, because I am an astute judge of character, John, as you know, that something bad had happened at training.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: I kind of saw the players trudging off with this look of "there but for the grace of God go I." They had seen something. I found out later that the something they had seen was a young player named Ibrahim Afellay had torn his ACL. And so I, of course, was not allowed to watch training. So I didn't see any of this. But I could sense something was wrong.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: And that is one of those things that I think really affects players' moods because they know that all of them are one bad turn, one injury like that, away from sitting out for a year. You know? And maybe, like in the case of Ibrahim Afellay--

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: And maybe never quite being the same.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Never quite being the same, exactly, which is precisely what happened to Afellay.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Anyway, at this point, it's past 6:00 PM. So I've been there for a full working day, nothing to eat, super hot. And I'm not one to be dramatic, John, but I was basically being held prisoner at the Barcelona training ground by that point. That's how it felt.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: So finally, it's just before 7:00 PM when the world's greatest player finally walks in. We sit down at this table. It's this little silver table. There's three chairs. It's me across from Messi. And his publicist is kind of in the middle. And so begins the world's worst interview. [LAUGHTER] It's like, he batted me away like-- I can't remember what I asked him, but he gave me this look like he'd rather be at the dentist.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: And just looking at me, and I'm disheveled and sweaty. My shirt was a normal size at the beginning of the day, but after eight hours of being held hostage at the Barcelona training ground in a hot September day, the shirt was just stuck to me. And I asked my first question. And he said this thing, and I'm going to imitate an Argentine accent. He said--

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: --which Is basically like, dude, I've been asked this so many times. He's rolling his eyes. And I'm just--

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: Oh God.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: And it got worse from there. It just got worse. I realize that something bad has happened at training. I realize that he's not interested in speaking with me. He doesn't know what a GQ is or what a Vogue is. He doesn't give a [BLEEP]. He doesn't care. He's just like, this weird guy who's all sweaty is sitting here. He's been waiting for me for eight hours, like a freaking stalker. And now he's asking me dumb questions that I've been asked before.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: And so he's just being monosyllabic. And at the end of it, it's just devastating. Basically, the publicist just kind of calls time on it, and it's done. Before he walks out, we take this photograph. I ask the publicist if it's OK if we take a photograph. And he said this thing to me. He's like, of course. I know we all have feelings.

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: We all have feelings?

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: The publicist can sense my humiliation, which is actually manifesting as physical pain. Like, at this point, it's just like this is the worst reporting experience of my life, possibly one of the most humiliating experiences of my life at all, of the whole of it. So I took my photo. Messi walks out, immediately, of course, forgets the entire interaction that I have never forgotten.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Needless to say, I wrote my draft and then got a very efficient, carefully-worded email from my editor saying that the article was not going to be published and that I could kindly take my kill fee and go away.

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: Brutal.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: John Green
segments.text: I don't know how to ask this delicately, but even on his best day, Lionel Messi is pretty at arms length when it comes to interviews. And in retrospect, there is something charming about the fact that you thought you were going to get the real Lionel Messi.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, he batted me aside like I was a third-tier defender and went on with his life. And so here I am thinking, man, we're going to vibe on this because we both have this deep emotional and deep intellectual understanding of the game. And basically what he was telling me was like, no, you're down here, and I'm up here.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Daniel and John's show is called The Away End, which is a soccer podcast about the run-up to the World Cup made by two people who really like books. Emmanuel Dzotsi produced this version for our show.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Our program was produced today by me and edited by David Kestenbaum. The people who put together today's show are Phia Bennin, Dana Chivvis, Cassie Howley, Adriene Lilly, Seth Lind, Molly Marcello, Katherine Rae Mondo, Stowe Nelson, Robin Reid, Ryan Rumery, Alissa Shipp, Christopher Swetala, Nancy Updike, and Diane Wu.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Our managing editor is Sarah Abdurrahman, and our executive editor is Emanuele Berry. Very special thanks today to Sam McKiniss. Thanks also to all This American Life partners. segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Thanks, as always, to our boss, Ira Glass. You know, at his own wedding recently, he decided it would be funny to start his vows by saying, "it's This American Wife." Nobody laughed.

segments.speaker: Daniel Alarcón
segments.text: It was just beginning to dawn on me that this was the wrong way to start my marriage.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I'm Ike Sriskandarajah. Ira Glass will be back next week with more stories of This American Life.
